title: Ilchester to Oxford's Grave: the Doctor Mirabilis and the Arabic Sciences
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Ilchester, birth into a house of means
stops.campa: In the small Somerset town of Ilchester, on the old Roman road above the river Yeo, Roger is born into a family of landed comfort, able to give a younger son the costliest gift a house of that century can give: an education. Ilchester's streets remember Rome before they remember England; its church bells ring over water-meadows where his father's cattle graze. No parish register marks the day, and later ages will argue his year by a decade either way, but tradition fixes it here, in this house, in this town, twelve hundred and fourteen.
suggested_refs: The site of Ilchester (Roman Lindinis), traditionally given as Bacon's birthplace
sources: Britannica, Roger Bacon
MacTutor History of Mathematics, Roger Bacon
Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), Roger Bacon

stops.name: Ilchester, sent to the schools at thirteen
stops.campa: At thirteen the boy is put on the road to Oxford, his father's purse behind him, to begin the trivium that opens every clerkly life: grammar, logic, rhetoric, the Latin that will outlast every kingdom he will ever see rise or fall. Somerset falls away behind the packhorse; eight years of the schools lie ahead before the quadrivium and a master's gown. He will remember, decades later and bitterly, how much of his family's wealth was spent to make him what he is about to become, and how little of it will be left when he most needs it.
suggested_refs: The medieval road from Somerset to Oxford, the common route of the county's clerks
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, Roger Bacon
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Roger Bacon

stops.name: Oxford, the shadow of Grosseteste in the schools
stops.campa: The schools of Oxford in these years stand under one great shadow: Robert Grosseteste, master of the arts faculty and first lector to the Franciscans newly settled in the town, who reads Aristotle's Physics through a mathematics of light no one in England has attempted before him. The young Bacon, still a boy among the trivium's grammar-benches, hears the name before he hears the argument. He will spend the rest of his working life, by his own later account, in the debt of this one man's method: that number and geometry are the door into nature, and that the door stands open.
suggested_refs: Robert Grosseteste's De Luce and De Iride, foundational texts of the Oxford light-metaphysics Bacon inherits
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Roger Bacon
MacTutor History of Mathematics, Roger Bacon

stops.name: Oxford, the quadrivium: number, geometry, music, the stars
stops.campa: Past the trivium's grammar and disputation, Bacon takes up the quadrivium: arithmetic, geometry, music, astronomy, the four roads by which the schools say the soul climbs toward the stable truths. He shows an early hunger for the mathematical arts beyond what the ordinary course demands, copying diagrams, tracing the geometry of the sphere. In later years he will call mathematics the gate and the key of all the other sciences, the one subject a student cannot fail to master before he dares approach the rest; the conviction is formed here, on these benches, years before he can prove it to anyone else.
stops.quote: Mathematics is the gate and key of the sciences... Neglect of mathematics works injury to all knowledge, since he who is ignorant of it cannot know the other sciences or the things of this world.
stops.quote_source: Opus Majus, Part IV, on the utility of mathematics (Bridges edition)
suggested_refs: Bacon's dictum on mathematics, cited across the historiography of medieval science
sources: Wikiquote, Roger Bacon (Opus Majus, Bridges edition)
MacTutor History of Mathematics, Roger Bacon

stops.name: Oxford, the master's gown
stops.campa: After some eight years in the schools Bacon is made a master of arts, licensed now to lecture in his own right at the University Church, to dispute publicly, to take fees from the sons of other men. He is, by every account of his own later temper, already impatient with the way the schools teach: too much repetition of authority, too little looking at the thing itself. The road from Oxford now bends toward Paris, where the arts faculty is larger, richer in books, and thick with the newly recovered natural philosophy of Aristotle that Oxford has only begun to absorb.
suggested_refs: The University Church of St Mary the Virgin, seat of the medieval Oxford schools and disputations
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, Roger Bacon
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Roger Bacon

stops.name: Paris, arrival on the rue du Fouarre
stops.campa: Bacon crosses to Paris and takes his place among the regent masters of the rue du Fouarre, the Street of Straw, where the arts faculty sits its students on bundled straw to hear lectures on logic and natural philosophy. The city holds more books, more masters, more argument than Oxford has ever gathered in one place; it is here, among foreigners and Frenchmen both, that an Englishman can become one of the great teachers of Aristotle in the West. He lectures, disputes, and begins to earn the reputation for encyclopedic reading that will follow him the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: The rue du Fouarre in the Latin Quarter, where the medieval arts faculty held its lectures
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, Roger Bacon
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Roger Bacon

stops.name: Paris, lecturing the forbidden books of nature
stops.campa: A generation before Bacon's regency, the bishops of Paris had banned Aristotle's libri naturales from the schools as dangerous novelty; by the 1240s the ban has worn thin, tolerated more than enforced, and Bacon reads the Physics and Metaphysics openly to his students, among the first masters anywhere to lecture the whole of the recovered Aristotelian corpus as ordinary university fare. He is already forming the judgment that will mark every later book: that the Latin translations he is forced to teach from are careless, sometimes unintelligible, and that the true text lies further back, in Greek and in Arabic, than any Paris copy reaches.
suggested_refs: The 1210s and 1231 Paris bans on Aristotle's natural philosophy, eroding by the time of Bacon's regency
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Roger Bacon
Daily Medieval, Roger Bacon's Opus Majus

stops.name: Paris, the Franciscan school of Alexander of Hales
stops.campa: Across the river from the arts faculty, the Franciscans have built their own school around the aging Alexander of Hales, the first of the order's masters to hold a chair in theology at Paris, and around it gathers the same fusion of piety and encyclopedic learning Bacon already prizes in Grosseteste at home. He watches the grey-robed friars debate with a freedom the secular masters do not always permit themselves, unbound by benefice or diocese, answerable only to their own general. Thirteen years before he takes the habit himself, the pattern of the life he will choose is already visible to him here.
suggested_refs: The Franciscan studium at Paris under Alexander of Hales, forerunner of Bacon's own order
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Roger Bacon
MacTutor History of Mathematics, Roger Bacon

stops.name: Paris, Peter Peregrinus, the master of experiment
stops.campa: Among the men Bacon meets in these Paris years, one stands apart from every master and every book: Peter Peregrinus, soldier and engineer, who tests the properties of the lodestone with his own hands rather than repeating what Aristotle or any commentator says of magnets. Bacon watches him work, indifferent to the wealth his skill could bring him, absorbed instead in what Bacon will later call the great experiments in which he delights. It is a revelation: a man who trusts the needle over the authority, and Bacon will spend the rest of his career trying to make an entire science out of that trust.
stops.quote: One man I know, and one only, who can be praised for his achievements in this science. Of discourses and battles of words he takes no heed: he follows the works of wisdom, and in these finds rest.
stops.quote_source: Opus Tertium, cap. 13, on the master of experiment, identified by Bridges as Petrus Peregrinus de Maricourt
suggested_refs: Peter Peregrinus's Epistola de magnete (1269), the earliest surviving treatise on magnetism
The dominus experimentorum passage of Opus Tertium cap. 13; the naming of Peregrinus survives as a marginal gloss in one manuscript
sources: Wikiquote, Roger Bacon (Bridges, The Opus Majus of Roger Bacon, 1900, vol. 1, preface p. xxv)
Wikipedia, Petrus Peregrinus de Maricourt

stops.name: Paris, the regency ends, the road home
stops.campa: After some seven years lecturing the arts at Paris, Bacon lays down his regency and turns back toward England, though not toward the schools he left. Something has shifted in him: less appetite for repeating disputed questions to boys learning logic, more for the unglossed text itself, the instrument in the hand, the observed thing. He carries back across the Channel a reputation as one of the widest-read men in either university, and a restlessness that the ordinary round of arts teaching can no longer satisfy.
suggested_refs: The Channel crossing between the two great thirteenth-century schools, Paris and Oxford
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, Roger Bacon
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Roger Bacon

segments.name: Oxford Again, the Secret Arts of Light

stops.name: Oxford, the inheritance spent on books and instruments
stops.campa: Back at Oxford and free of the arts-faculty round, Bacon turns his family's remaining money into an instrument of research: rare manuscripts bought at any price, lenses ground and mirrors cast, astronomical tables copied by hired scribes, alchemical apparatus assembled in rooms that smell of furnace-smoke. He will later reckon the sum at above two thousand pounds, a fortune, spent across these years on what he calls the secret books and experiments of the sciences. His family's fortune is not inexhaustible, and he knows it even as he spends; but no other Latin scholar of his day owns what his money is now buying him.
stops.quote: I have labored much in sciences and languages, and I have up to now devoted forty years [to them] after I first learned the Alphabetum; and I was always studious.
stops.quote_source: Opus Tertium, on his years of self-directed research (OQHI 65, as translated by Hackett)
suggested_refs: Bacon's own later reckoning of the sums spent on books, instruments, and secret experiment
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, Roger Bacon
Encyclopedia.com, Roger Bacon

stops.name: Oxford, friendship with Adam Marsh
stops.campa: In the Franciscan school at Oxford, Bacon comes to know Adam Marsh, Grosseteste's own favored pupil and now the order's leading English theologian, a man of such reputation that kings and bishops write to him for counsel. Marsh's learning is wide, careful, unshowy, exactly the temper Bacon prizes; where the ordinary schoolman piles authority on authority, Marsh and his circle test a thing before they teach it. Bacon will later name Marsh, alongside Grosseteste, among the very few men of his century he is willing to call perfect in the sciences.
suggested_refs: The Oxford Greyfriars school library, where Marsh and later Bacon both taught
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Roger Bacon
MacTutor History of Mathematics, Roger Bacon

stops.name: Oxford, the Book of Optics of Ibn al-Haytham
stops.campa: Among the manuscripts his money has bought him, none occupies Bacon more than the Latin De Aspectibus, the translation of Ibn al-Haytham's Kitab al-Manazir, written two centuries before in Cairo and carried west through Toledo's translators. Here is a science of vision built not on Aristotle's authority but on controlled experiment with darkened chambers, pinholes, and measured angles of reflection and refraction: exactly the method Bacon has been reaching for without a name for it. He works through the whole of the known Greek and Arabic literature on perspectiva that the century has made available, and begins to see how a true optics might be built.
stops.quote: There are two ways of acquiring knowledge, one through reason, the other by experiment.
stops.quote_source: Opus Majus, Part VI, on scientia experimentalis
suggested_refs: The Latin De Aspectibus, the translation of Ibn al-Haytham's Kitab al-Manazir that shaped all of Bacon's optics
sources: Muslim Heritage, The Attraction of Ibn al-Haytham's Optics
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Roger Bacon

stops.name: Oxford, the death of Grosseteste, the corpus of light inherited
stops.campa: Word reaches Oxford that Robert Grosseteste, Bishop of Lincoln, has died at his manor at Buckden: the man whose writings on light, the rainbow, and the multiplication of species have shaped nearly everything Bacon has attempted since boyhood. There is no living teacher left of that first rank in England. Bacon gathers what remains in manuscript, the treatises on optics and the calendar Grosseteste never lived to finish reforming, and treats them from this day as the foundation on which his own science of perspectiva and his own case to Rome for a reformed calendar will both be built.
suggested_refs: Robert Grosseteste's collected scientific treatises, De Iride and De Lineis, Angulis et Figuris
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Roger Bacon
MacTutor History of Mathematics, Roger Bacon

stops.name: Oxford, Folly Bridge, the tower and the tale of the brazen head
stops.campa: Above the south gate of the town, on the bridge over the Thames, Bacon keeps a hexagonal study for his stargazing and his instruments; the tower stands for five hundred years after him under the name Friar Bacon's Study before the widening road takes it down. It is here, in the tales that gather around these years of furnace and lens and midnight observation, that he and Friar Bungay are said to labor seven years over a head cast in brass, meaning to make it speak and wall all England in a rampart no enemy could breach. The head speaks once, they say, and no one is awake to hear it.
suggested_refs: Friar Bacon's Study at Folly Bridge (demolished 1779); Robert Greene's Friar Bacon and Friar Bungay, which fixed the brazen head's three words in legend
sources: cabinet.ox.ac.uk, Friar Bacon's Study and Folly Bridge
Wikipedia, Brazen head
Icy Sedgwick, The Brazen Head: Medieval Prophecy Machine or Tall Tale?

segments.name: The Grey Habit, the Silenced Years

stops.name: Oxford, the Franciscan vows
stops.campa: Bacon takes the grey habit of the Friars Minor, drawn as he later says by the example of Grosseteste, Marsh, and the other English Franciscans who first showed him that holiness and hard science need not stand apart. It is not yet clear to him what the choice will cost: an order vowed to poverty and obedience has its own chapters, its own generals, its own opinion of what a friar may write and to whom. He does not yet know that the decade now opening will be, in his own later word, one of exile from the work he was made for.
suggested_refs: The grey habit of the Order of Friars Minor, Bacon's dress for the rest of his life
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Roger Bacon
MacTutor History of Mathematics, Roger Bacon

stops.name: Paris, the Constitutions of Narbonne, the ban on publishing
stops.campa: The order's general chapter, meeting under Bonaventure at Narbonne, tightens a rule first aimed at the heretical writings of Gerard of Borgo San Donnino: no friar may publish any work outside the order without the express license of his superiors. Bacon, moved about this time to the Paris convent under the eye of the English Franciscan Richard of Cornwall, finds himself bound by exactly the rule his own restless, encyclopedic temperament is least suited to obey. He goes on working; he simply can no longer send what he writes beyond the friary walls.
suggested_refs: The Constitutions of Narbonne (1260), Bonaventure's tightening of Franciscan publication discipline
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Roger Bacon
New World Encyclopedia, Roger Bacon

stops.name: Paris, the years of silence
stops.campa: For years now Bacon works inside the Paris convent with no outlet for what he produces: burdened, he will later complain, with duties outside his own study, watched, and kept from correspondence with the scholars whose work he most needs to test his own against. He will write, years afterward and still smarting, that his superiors forced him with unspeakable violence to obey their will, against every instinct of his own vocation. Whatever science he manages in these years exists only in his own hand, unread by anyone who might carry it further.
stops.quote: They forced me with unspeakable violence to obey their will.
stops.quote_source: Opus Tertium, recalling the years of restriction under his Franciscan superiors
suggested_refs: Opus Tertium's retrospective account of the silenced decade, Bacon's own bitterest complaint
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, Roger Bacon
New World Encyclopedia, Roger Bacon

stops.name: Paris, a correspondence begins with Guy le Gros de Foulques
stops.campa: Somewhere in these silenced years Bacon comes to the notice of Cardinal Guy le Gros de Foulques, papal legate, a churchman of wide sympathy for reform who asks the friar, informally and outside any official channel, to set down his thinking on the state of learning and of Christendom. Bacon cannot comply while the ban on publication stands, but he does not forget the request; it is the one thread, among all the walls his own order has built around him, that still leads outward toward Rome. He waits, and writes what he can in private, against the day the cardinal might be able to ask him formally.
suggested_refs: Cardinal Guy le Gros de Foulques, later Pope Clement IV, whose informal request Bacon could not yet answer
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Roger Bacon
Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), Roger Bacon

segments.name: The Pope's Mandate: the Opus Majus

stops.name: Viterbo, the mandate of Clement IV
stops.campa: From the half-built papal palace at Viterbo, where Clement IV keeps the curia because Rome itself is too hostile to enter, a letter goes out under the pope's own seal to Brother Roger Bacon: send, and send secretly, notwithstanding any constitution of your order to the contrary, the writings you spoke of to us before our elevation. It is the single document that breaks every wall the Narbonne chapter raised. Bacon, still bound and watched in Paris, now has what no rule of his superiors can override: a direct papal command, addressed to him alone.
suggested_refs: Clement IV's mandate of 22 June 1266, issued from the Palazzo dei Papi at Viterbo
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), Roger Bacon
Wikipedia, Pope Clement IV
Wikipedia, Palace of the Popes in Viterbo

stops.name: Paris, secret composition, a house too poor to pay for parchment
stops.campa: Bacon sets to work at once, in secret from his own brothers, on the encyclopedic case the pope has asked for. But the family fortune that once bought him books and instruments is gone, swallowed the previous year when the Second Barons' War broke over England and de Montfort's men and the king's men between them ruined the estates of families like his own. He has no money for scribes or parchment, and is reduced to begging loans from friends and poor students, promising them repayment of sixty pounds out of whatever the pope may see fit to send him.
suggested_refs: The Second Barons' War (1264-65) and the ruin it brought to royalist families like Bacon's own
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), Roger Bacon
MacTutor History of Mathematics, Roger Bacon

stops.name: Paris, the Opus Majus finished, the four causes of error
stops.campa: In a matter of months Bacon completes the Opus Majus, some eight hundred pages arguing the unity of all true knowledge: the obstacles that keep men from wisdom, the necessity of Greek, Hebrew, and Arabic to read Scripture and philosophy without the errors of careless translators, mathematics as the door to every other science, and beneath it all a plain accusation against the schools that raised him. Weak authority, long custom, the opinion of the ignorant crowd, and the hiding of one's own ignorance behind a show of learning: these four, he writes, are what keep Christendom from the truth it already half possesses.
stops.quote: the example of frail and unfit authority, long custom, the sense of the ignorant crowd, and the concealment of one's own ignorance with a display of apparent wisdom
stops.quote_source: Opus Majus, Part I, cap. 1, the four offendicula: auctoritatis fragilis et indignae exemplum, consuetudinis diuturnitas, vulgi sensus imperiti, et propriae ignorantiae occultatio cum ostentatione sapientiae apparentis
suggested_refs: The Opus Majus manuscript, its Part I on the causes of error among the most quoted pages of medieval philosophy
sources: Richard Smith's blog, Roger Bacon on ignorance and peer review
Wikisource, Opus Majus (Bridges edition)

stops.name: Paris, the geometry of light, the rainbow measured
stops.campa: Within the same great work Bacon lays out the perspectiva he built from Ibn al-Haytham's optics and his own instruments: the anatomy of the eye, the geometry of reflection and refraction, a description of lenses that could, rightly ground, bring far things near. He works out the altitude of the rainbow's arc by careful measurement and gives instructions, half a description and half a prophecy, for a device that would let a man see things at a great distance as though they stood beside him. No one in Paris or Oxford has attempted to make experimental geometry answer for the sky in quite this way before.
suggested_refs: Bacon's calculation of the rainbow's altitude at roughly 42 degrees, and his description of a telescope-like instrument
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, Roger Bacon
Muslim Heritage, The Attraction of Ibn al-Haytham's Optics

stops.name: Paris, the Opus Minus, the Opus Tertium, and the calendar's error
stops.campa: Fearing the great bulk of the Opus Majus may be lost or unread, Bacon writes a shorter Opus Minus to recapitulate it, and then a longer Opus Tertium besides, restating his case and adding what the first work left out: among it, a demonstration that the Julian calendar has drifted so far from the true solar year that Easter itself is calculated wrong, an error he calls intolerable, horrible, and laughable, and a proposed correction anticipating by three centuries the reform Pope Gregory will eventually make. Into the same packet, later tradition holds, he folds a cipher describing how saltpetre, charcoal, and sulphur together make a fire that roars and leaps.
stops.quote_source: Opus Majus, Part IV, on the accumulated error of the Julian calendar
suggested_refs: The calendar reform proposed in Opus Majus Part IV; the disputed gunpowder cipher of the Epistola de secretis operibus
sources: Wikipedia, Opus Majus
JAWChemist blog, Translation of Roger Bacon's Gunpowder Formula

stops.name: Viterbo, the manuscript arrives, the burning mirror is shown
stops.campa: Bacon's pupil, a young friar the record calls John, carries the finished bundle south across France and Italy to Viterbo: the Opus Majus, the Opus Minus, drawings of lenses and a burning mirror, and instructions for demonstrating each to the Holy Father in person. John is charged to answer whatever questions the pope may put, since Bacon himself cannot travel. Whether Clement IV, already ailing, ever reads the whole of what has been sent him, the canon does not record; what it does record is that the friar's work has, for the first time in a decade, left his own hand and reached the one reader who asked for it.
suggested_refs: The Palazzo dei Papi at Viterbo, where the Opus Majus was delivered in 1267
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), Roger Bacon
MacTutor History of Mathematics, Roger Bacon

stops.name: Viterbo, Santa Maria in Gradi, the death of Clement IV
stops.campa: Clement IV dies at Viterbo and is laid in the Dominican church of Santa Maria in Gradi outside the walls, and with him dies every hope Bacon had of a curia bent to his reforms. No successor is elected for nearly three years; the office that alone stood above the Narbonne rule and could compel his own order to hear him now sits empty. Bacon, back in Paris or already returning to Oxford, is left once more with only his own pen, his own conviction, and no mandate from anyone to protect either.
suggested_refs: The tomb of Clement IV at Santa Maria in Gradi, Viterbo
sources: Wikipedia, Pope Clement IV
Wikipedia, Palace of the Popes in Viterbo

segments.name: Oxford, the Compendium and the Widening Quarrel

stops.name: Oxford, the Communia Naturalium and Communia Mathematica
stops.campa: Without a pope now to answer to, Bacon returns to the slower, more patient labor of building the whole encyclopedia of the sciences he had only sketched for Clement: the Communia Naturalium and the Communia Mathematica, works meant to lay the entire philosophy of nature on a mathematical and experimental footing, chapter by chapter, from first principles. Neither work is ever finished; both break off mid-argument, as though the friar always had one more objection to raise against himself before he could call a question closed. He restates, in these unfinished pages, the same conviction that has carried him since Paris: argument alone settles nothing the mind can fully trust.
stops.quote: Argument reaches a conclusion and compels us to admit it, but it neither makes us certain, nor does it remove doubt so that the mind may rest in the intuition of truth, unless it finds this certitude by way of experience.
stops.quote_source: Opus Majus, Part VI, on the necessity of experimental science
suggested_refs: The unfinished Communia Naturalium and Communia Mathematica, Bacon's attempt at a complete natural philosophy
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Roger Bacon
James Lind Library, Bacon, Roger (1266)

stops.name: Oxford, the Compendium Studii Philosophiae, the call to Arabic
stops.campa: In the Compendium Studii Philosophiae Bacon turns his old complaint into open attack: the schools are ruled by ignorant masters and worse translators, and Latin Christendom, if it wishes to possess the sciences at all, must go and learn Greek, Hebrew, and Arabic and read the philosophers, physicians, and mathematicians of Islam in their own tongue rather than in the mangled Latin now passed off as their thought. He names no colleague kindly; the tract reads as a general indictment of an entire century's scholarship, and it earns him, among the men it names, exactly the enemies such a book would be expected to make.
suggested_refs: The Compendium Studii Philosophiae's demand that Latin scholars master the Arabic sciences at their source
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Roger Bacon
MacTutor History of Mathematics, Roger Bacon

stops.name: Paris, the condemnation of the two hundred and nineteen articles
stops.campa: The Bishop of Paris, Étienne Tempier, publishes a condemnation of two hundred and nineteen propositions drawn from the arts faculty's teaching, aimed chiefly at the radical Aristotelians but casting suspicion over any master who reasons too freely about the stars' influence on human affairs or the limits placed on divine power by natural law. Bacon has never taught at Paris under this bishop, but the atmosphere the condemnation creates reaches every province of the order: astrology, judicial prediction, and unlicensed natural philosophy are, for the first time in a generation, matters a friar had better not be caught defending too boldly.
suggested_refs: The Condemnation of 1277, Bishop Tempier's list of 219 forbidden propositions
sources: Wikipedia, Roger Bacon
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Roger Bacon

stops.name: Paris, the general chapter condemns Bacon's teaching
stops.campa: Jerome of Ascoli, Minister General of the Franciscan Order and later Pope Nicholas IV, calls Bacon's teaching to account for certain suspected novelties, the chronicle's own phrase, and condemns it before the assembled friars. What exactly stands condemned the record never says outright: his combative Compendium and its long list of enemies, his interest in astrology and in the prophecies then circulating among the order's more radical wing, or some other doctrine now lost, are all named by later scholars as the likely cause. Whatever the charge, the sentence that follows is the harshest an order can pass on one of its own without unfrocking him.
stops.quote_source: Chronicle of the Twenty-four Generals of the Franciscan Order (14th century), on the condemnation of Bacon's teaching
suggested_refs: The Chronicle of the Twenty-four Generals, the sole medieval source for Bacon's condemnation and imprisonment
sources: Encyclopedia.com, Roger Bacon
Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, Bacon, Roger

stops.name: Ancona, the sentence carried out
stops.campa: Tradition sends Bacon south to the Franciscan house at Ancona, on the Adriatic shore, to serve out the general's sentence far from Paris and Oxford both, watched, without students, without the pen he has never in his life gone long without. The friary keeps him as a body keeps a fever: contained, unremarked outside its own walls, its books and instruments left behind him in England and France. Whatever science occupies his mind in this room, none of it reaches parchment that survives; the busiest writer of his generation falls, for the only extended stretch of his life, silent.
suggested_refs: Ancona's Franciscan house, traditionally named as the place of Bacon's confinement
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, Roger Bacon
Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, Bacon, Roger

stops.name: Ancona, the years pass without a book
stops.campa: Years accumulate in the confinement the tradition describes, and no reliable chronicle troubles to record what fills them: whether Bacon is allowed his books at all, whether he is permitted to say Mass, whether news of Oxford or Paris reaches him even secondhand. Later ages, uncomfortable with so total a silence around so voluble a man, will fill the gap with legend, imagining him still grinding lenses, still calculating the calendar's drift in his head for want of a page to write it on. The canon itself offers only the bare fact of the years passing and the man, somewhere, still alive inside them.
suggested_refs: The near-total documentary silence surrounding Bacon's years of confinement, noted by every modern biographer
sources: Wikipedia, Roger Bacon
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Roger Bacon

segments.name: Release, the Last Book, and Oxford's Grave

stops.name: Oxford, release under Raymond of Gaufredi
stops.campa: A new Minister General, Raymond of Gaufredi, more sympathetic to the order's scholars than Jerome of Ascoli had been, lifts whatever restraint has held Bacon these dozen years, and the old friar, well past seventy now by any reckoning of his birth year, returns to the Oxford convent he first entered as a young master of arts. Little in him has softened; he takes up his pen again as though no years had intervened, though what he now writes is quieter, more concerned with settling accounts with theology than with winning new arguments in natural philosophy.
suggested_refs: Raymond of Gaufredi, Minister General of the Franciscans from 1289, credited with Bacon's release
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, Roger Bacon
Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, Bacon, Roger

stops.name: Oxford, the Compendium Studii Theologiae, the last book
stops.campa: In what will be his final work, the Compendium Studii Theologiae, Bacon takes care this time to distinguish plainly what he has always practiced from what his enemies accused him of: his physics from divination, his study of the stars from judicial astrology, his chemistry from the fraud of common alchemists. It is the plea of a man who knows exactly how his life's work has been misread and wants the record, before he can no longer correct it himself, to say plainly that everything in it was done in the light and for the Church, not against either. The manuscript breaks off unfinished.
suggested_refs: The unfinished Compendium Studii Theologiae, Bacon's final defense of the orthodoxy of his own science
sources: Encyclopedia.com, Roger Bacon
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Roger Bacon

stops.name: Oxford, the Greyfriars, death and burial
stops.campa: Roger Bacon dies at the Oxford Greyfriars, the same convent whose habit he took some five and thirty years before, and is buried within its walls among the brothers he had spent so much of his life in argument with. The friary itself will not outlast him by three centuries; it is suppressed in the dissolution and its stones scattered, so that no grave, no tomb, no plaque marks where Doctor Mirabilis was laid. What survives is the paper: the Opus Majus, the unfinished Communia, the Compendium, and around all of it the slower-growing legend of the wonder-working friar and his head of speaking brass.
suggested_refs: The vanished Oxford Greyfriars, site of Bacon's burial, dissolved in 1538
The death year: modern scholarship gives c. 1292; the older tradition, followed by the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia, gives 11 June 1294
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, Roger Bacon
Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, Bacon, Roger
Wikipedia, Roger Bacon
